title: We Can Change the Topology: Reflex-Policy Control for Real-Time Reconfiguration of Photovoltaic Generators Under Partial Shading
content: A partially shaded photovoltaic generator loses power for a structural reason that no optimiser can remove: in a series connection every element carries the same current, so the weakest string throttles the whole panel. A maximum-power-point tracker optimises the operating point of the topology it is given; it cannot remove a shaded string from that topology. This paper argues, and quantifies, a different starting point, the topology itself is a controllable variable, and it can be changed in real time, locally, and under an explicit safety authorisation. The objective throughout is the highest power the panel can give under whatever shading is present, so that changing the circuit and deliberately leaving it alone are both outcomes of the same evaluation. We formalise this as a Reflex-Policy contract: local physical evidence is conditioned into a small number of low-bit states, a deterministic rule map proposes at most one bounded action, a supervisory layer authorises or refuses it against converter and safety constraints, the action changes the electrical topology, and the response is verified before control returns to the conventional optimiser. The decision path is galvanically and functionally separated from the power path and never carries harvesting current. The contract is instantiated on a common 3x3 photovoltaic benchmark through three decision technologies. The first is a binary non-volatile rule map held in a commercial MRAM device (Everspin MR25H00 class) addressed over SPI by an STM32 controller; the hardware chain, rule map, firmware state machine, protected actuation and bench validation protocol are fully defined and built. The second is a four-input, four-output, four-level crossbar inference block, evaluated by behavioural simulation because the physical multilevel board was not available. The third is an implementation in conventional electronics, comparators, mixed-signal conditioning, MCU, CPLD or FPGA, which is the route with immediate industrial availability. Across ten canonical static shading conditions the model gives a total of 6.175 W for the conventional fixed topology, 10.762 W for the best protected topology without converter gating (+74.3%) and 10.697 W once the minimum converter input voltage guard is enforced (+73.2%). The 1.1-point difference is not a loss of performance but the visible cost of a correct refusal: in one irregular case the guard inhibits an action that would have driven the converter input below its limit. In the chain containing the four-level inference block, representative dynamic sequences retain approximately +31.5%, +29.0% and +26.6% total gain for 20 ms, 100 ms and 200 ms of added decision and readout latency. These are model results. A first bench campaign on the binary implementation is reported in Section 10 against the model prediction case by case: every behavioural criterion passes, the acting cases return between 16% and 17% less gain than modelled with every deviation in the same direction, and the command reaches the driver in 9.55 ms against a pre-registered 100 ms limit. Those percentages are ratios of power held while a given shadow is present, not energy gains over an operating period. The measurements are preliminary and a second campaign is planned. A second criterion runs through this paper, and we believe it should run through any work that claims an energy benefit: the energy return on the energy invested. A control layer that recovers energy is worth building only if what it delivers decisively exceeds what it costs to sense, decide, switch and manufacture. Here that criterion is not an audit applied at the end; it shapes the design. It is why the decision is reduced to a few bits and one bounded action rather than made as capable as possible, and why the choice among rule-map technologies is settled by standby and embodied energy rather than by inference capability. We report no EROEI figure, because both terms of the ratio must be measured rather than assumed, and the bench criteria therefore include the energy consumed by the decision and actuation layer over the same sequences used for the energy comparison. Partial shading is among the most heavily studied loss mechanisms in photovoltaics, with a literature spanning tracking, bypass protection, interconnection reconfiguration and distributed conversion. Tracking optimises within a fixed circuit; bypass diodes divert conduction passively at a device threshold; array reconfiguration optimises interconnection patterns on slow horizons; distributed power electronics absorb the mismatch by adding a converter per module. Across that work the topology is something to optimise over, to protect against, or to work around, and to our knowledge no one reports the combination proposed here: a converter-input constraint on the action, an explicit permission envelope, refusal as a recorded outcome, and verification of the measured response against the expected one. That is where the energy reported here comes from: without the real-time topology change there is no gain of this kind to be had. The central observation about implementation is that the static energy ceiling is set by the topology and by the safety gate, not by the technology that stores the rule. Binary MRAM, multilevel crossbar and classical logic that select the same authorised one-hot action produce the same reconfigured circuit. What the decision technology changes is the time to the first safe action, the standby energy of the rule map and the qualification path, not the physics of the recovered power. This is what makes the architecture genuinely technology-agnostic, and it is why an industrial deployment can start with conventional European electronics while emerging non-volatile logic remains a roadmap option.
